title: A day built on prayer
hookLine: the five prayers as the frame of every day
tomorrow: one line in the dawn call isn't in any other. which one?

cards: Sunday night, a fresh planner, and every hour gets a color: class in blue, shifts in green, the gym in orange. By Wednesday the colors have bled into each other.

Here's a much older schedule, and the story of how it was set. In a report kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, on the night of his ascension, is given fifty prayers a day for his people.
On the way down he meets Moses, who asks what he was given. Fifty, he says. And Moses answers: your people won't be able to bear it.

teach.b: So he goes back, and the number drops. Moses sends him back again, and again, until it reaches five. Even then Moses says ask once more, and the Prophet says he's too shy to ask again.
Then the word comes: they are five, and they are fifty. Five to keep, with the reward of fifty.
Those five are the frame Muslims build a day on: Fajr at dawn, Dhuhr at midday, 'Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib at sunset, 'Isha at night.
The Qur'an puts it plainly, in Pickthall's words: "Lo! worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours. Not whenever a minute opens up.
Notice what that does to the planner. A lot of schedules start with the work and squeeze everything else into the gaps.
This one starts with five posts driven into the ground, and the day gets built between them: class between Fajr and Dhuhr, a shift from Dhuhr to 'Asr.
The posts move with the sun, a little earlier or later as the seasons turn, so the day keeps checking the sky and not only the clock.
And the story leaves one detail worth telling a friend tonight: the five came out of a conversation, with Moses pushing for mercy. For the next two weeks, this block walks the day one post at a time.

how: Muslims pray five daily prayers at times set by the sun: Fajr, Dhuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha. A mosque timetable or a prayer-time app gives each day's times, and people plan work, school and sleep around them.

games.q: what does “a day built on prayer” mean?
o: a day given entirely to prayer, with no work in it at all
a day framed by five fixed prayers, the rest built between
a day that opens with one prayer and then moves along

games.q: which post, which part of the day — tap the pairs.

s: in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the daily prayers began as fifty
Moses sent the Prophet back again and again until it reached five: five to keep, with the reward of fifty.
the Qur'an says to pray whenever you find a free minute
it says worship at fixed hours. the prayers are posts, not gap-fillers.
the prayers sit at the same clock time all year
they follow the sun, so the posts drift earlier or later as the seasons turn.

games.q: your study group books a long Saturday session, one to five. you pray. what does a day built on prayer suggest?
o: skip 'Asr this once; studying is a good deed too.
plan the session with the 'Asr break already in it.
pray every prayer early that morning to clear the afternoon.
games.why: the posts go in first and the work fits between them. fixed hours means the prayer isn't moved to make room; the session is.

practice: Take tomorrow, the real one, and find its five posts: about when dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night fall where you live. Put the five in first, then set your one biggest task between two of them, and notice what shifts.
If you pray, those are your five; if not, they can be five short pauses.

wordCard.voice: A day built on prayer: five fixed posts from dawn to night, set in the story of fifty becoming five, and everything else fitted in between.

orig.note: Arabic: the ritual prayer, kept five times a day at fixed hours.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: the day has a frame, five posts first and the rest built between. Block D, begun.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 (the ascension; fifty prayers reduced to five at Moses' urging; 'they are five and they are fifty')
